title: Personal Task Tracker
description: Build a simple CRUD task manager with categories, due dates, and drag-to-reorder. Focus on clean UI, accessible forms, and data persistence.

requirements.body: Create, read, update, and delete tasks
Assign each task a category and an optional due date
Mark tasks as complete; completed tasks move to a separate view
Filter tasks by category and sort by due date or creation time
Drag-to-reorder tasks within a category
Fully responsive — usable on mobile and desktop
Accessible: keyboard navigable, ARIA labels on all controls
State persisted across page reloads (localStorage or REST API)
Initial page load under 2 seconds on a slow 3G connection

items: Build task list and task card components in React
Implement controlled forms for task creation and editing
Wire category filter and sort controls to local state
Integrate a drag-and-drop library (e.g. @hello-pangea/dnd)
Persist tasks in localStorage
Design a REST API with endpoints for CRUD operations on tasks
Add JSON Schema validation for task creation and update payloads
Implement filtering and sorting at the query level
Write unit tests for all API handlers
Implement the complete feature end-to-end (UI + API + persistence)
Choose between localStorage-only or a full REST API + DB approach
Ensure the UI and API stay in sync after each mutation
Deploy to a free tier host (Vercel + Neon, or Railway)

steps.title: Scaffold the project
steps.body:
Open your terminal and run:

```bash
npm create vite@latest task-tracker -- --template react
cd task-tracker
npm install
npm run dev
```

You should see a starter React page in your browser. Delete everything inside `src/App.jsx` so you have a blank slate.

steps.title: Plan your data shape on paper first
steps.body:
Before writing any code, write out what one task looks like as an object:

```js
{ id, title, category, dueDate, completed, order, createdAt }
```

Every field should have a reason. `id` is for uniquely identifying tasks. `order` is for drag-to-reorder. Do this step — skipping it causes rewrites later.

steps.title: Render hardcoded tasks to the screen
steps.body:
In `App.jsx`, create a tasks array with 2 or 3 tasks written out by hand: ```js const tasks = [ { id: 1, title: 'First task', category: 'Work' }, { id: 2, title: 'Second task', category: 'Personal' } ] ``` Map over the array and render each task title in a `
  • `: ```jsx
      {tasks.map(task => (
    • {task.title}
      • ))}
    ``` This proves your render loop works before you touch state or forms.

steps.title: Build a TaskItem component
steps.body:
Create `src/components/TaskItem.jsx`. It receives one task object as a prop and displays the title, category, and due date. No buttons, no logic — just display.

Import it into `App.jsx` and use it inside your map. Keep components small and focused on one job.

steps.title: Move tasks into useState
steps.body:
Replace your static tasks with:

```js
const [tasks, setTasks] = useState([...your hardcoded tasks...])
```

Nothing on screen should change. `useState` means React will re-render whenever you call `setTasks`. You need this before you can add, delete, or edit tasks.

steps.title: Build the create task form
steps.body:
Create `src/components/AddTaskForm.jsx` with a controlled input for title, a select for category, and a date input for due date.

On submit, call a function passed down as a prop (e.g. `onAdd`).

In `App.jsx`, write the `onAdd` function:

```js
setTasks([
  ...tasks,
  {
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),
    title,
    category,
    dueDate,
    completed: false,
    order: tasks.length,
    createdAt: new Date()
  }
])
```

steps.title: Add delete
steps.body:
Pass an `onDelete` prop to TaskItem. Add a Delete button inside TaskItem that calls `onDelete(task.id)` when clicked.

In `App.jsx`, write the handler:

```js
setTasks(tasks.filter(t => t.id !== id))
```

Test it — clicking delete should remove just that task from the list.

steps.title: Add complete toggle
steps.body:
Add a checkbox at the start of each TaskItem. When it changes, call an `onToggle(task.id)` prop.

In `App.jsx`:

```js
setTasks(tasks.map(t =>
  t.id === id
    ? { ...t, completed: !t.completed }
    : t
))
```

The spread `{ ...t }` copies all existing fields — you only override `completed`.

steps.title: Split active and completed views
Add category filter
steps.body:
Add state:

```js
const [filterCategory, setFilterCategory] = useState('all')
```

Render a `<select>` that lists all unique categories plus an 'All' option.

Before rendering activeTasks, filter them:

```js
const visible = filterCategory === 'all'
  ? activeTasks
  : activeTasks.filter(t => t.category === filterCategory)
```

steps.title: Add sort controls
steps.body:
Add state:

```js
const [sortBy, setSortBy] = useState('createdAt')
```

Sort before rendering:

```js
const sorted = [...visible].sort((a, b) =>
  sortBy === 'dueDate'
    ? new Date(a.dueDate) - new Date(b.dueDate)
    : new Date(a.createdAt) - new Date(b.createdAt)
)
```

Always sort a copy (`[...visible]`) — never mutate state directly.

steps.title: Persist to localStorage
Add drag-to-reorder
steps.body:
Run:

```bash
npm install @hello-pangea/dnd
```

Wrap your list in drag-and-drop components and handle reordering using `result.source.index` and `result.destination.index`.

requirements.body: Search for weather by city name with a debounced input
Display current temperature, conditions, humidity, and wind speed
Show a 5-day forecast with daily high/low

Support geolocation to auto-detect current city on load
Allow up to 5 saved favourite locations
API key must never be exposed in client-side code
API responses cached for 5 minutes to reduce upstream calls
Graceful error states for invalid city or network failure
Mobile responsive with touch-friendly chart interactions

Render current weather card and 5-day forecast cards
Integrate Chart.js or Recharts for temperature/humidity graphs
Implement Geolocation API with user-permission prompt
Store saved locations in localStorage and sync to UI
Create a proxy endpoint that forwards requests to OpenWeatherMap
Implement in-memory response caching with a 5-minute TTL
Add IP-based rate limiting to the proxy endpoint
Return structured error responses for unknown cities or API failures

steps.title: Get your API key and read the docs
steps.body:
Sign up at openweathermap.org and get a free API key. The free tier allows 60 calls/minute — plenty for development.

Open the One Call API 3.0 docs and read the response shape carefully. The response has three top-level arrays you'll use:

- `current` — current conditions
- `hourly` — 48-hour forecast, one entry per hour
- `daily` — 8-day forecast, one entry per day

Before writing any React, confirm you can hit the API directly:

```bash
curl "https://api.openweathermap.org/data/3.0/onecall
  ?lat=51.51&lon=-0.13
  &exclude=minutely,alerts
  &units=metric
  &appid=YOUR_API_KEY"
```

Paste the response into a JSON formatter and study the `current`, `hourly[0]`, and `daily[0]` shapes — your normaliser in Step 3 will be based on exactly this structure.

Do not proceed until you get a `200` back and understand what each field means.

steps.title: Scaffold a Fastify proxy server
steps.body:
Your API key must never be shipped to the browser. The solution is a thin proxy server that holds the key server-side and forwards requests to OWM.

Create a Fastify server with a single endpoint:

```http
GET /weather?city=London
```

Store your key in `.env` and load it with `dotenv`:

```js
import Fastify from 'fastify'
import 'dotenv/config'

const app = Fastify()

app.get('/weather', async (request, reply) => {
  const { city } = request.query
  const geoUrl = `http://api.openweathermap.org/geo/1.0/direct?q=${city}&limit=1&appid=${process.env.OWM_KEY}`
  const [location] = await fetch(geoUrl).then(r => r.json())

  const url = `https://api.openweathermap.org/data/3.0/onecall?lat=${location.lat}&lon=${location.lon}&exclude=minutely,alerts&units=metric&appid=${process.env.OWM_KEY}`
  const data = await fetch(url).then(r => r.json())

  return data
})

app.listen({ port: 3001 })
```

Return the raw OWM response for now — you'll normalise it in Step 3. Test with curl before moving on.

steps.title: Normalise the API response
Add server-side caching
Add rate limiting and error handling
Build the search input with debounce
Build the current weather card
steps.body:
Create a `WeatherCard` component that receives the normalised `current` object as a prop. Build it with hardcoded mock data first so you can style it before touching the API: ```jsx function WeatherCard({ current }) { const iconUrl = `https://openweathermap.org/img/wn/${current.icon}@2x.png` return (
{current.temp}°C
{current.condition}
Feels like {current.feelsLike}°C {current.humidity}% humidity {current.windSpeed} m/s wind
) } ``` OWM icon codes follow the pattern `{icon}@2x.png` for double-resolution. The `@2x` variant is 100×100px — enough for a card but use `@4x` if your card is larger than 80px. Once the card looks right with mock data, replace the hardcoded object with the real API response.

steps.title: Build the 5-day forecast row
Add the temperature and humidity chart
steps.body:
Install `recharts`.

Create a `TemperatureChart` component that takes the `hourly` array (24 entries) as a prop.

Use:

```jsx
import { ResponsiveContainer, LineChart, Line, XAxis, Tooltip } from 'recharts'

function TemperatureChart({ hourly }) {
  const data = hourly.map(h => ({
    time:     new Date(h.time).getHours() + ':00',
    temp:     h.temp,
    humidity: h.humidity,
  }))

  return (
    <ResponsiveContainer width="100%" height={200}>
      <LineChart data={data}>
        <XAxis dataKey="time" interval={3} />
        <Tooltip />
        <Line dataKey="temp" stroke="#f97316" dot={false} />
        <Line dataKey="humidity" stroke="#3b82f6" dot={false} />
      </LineChart>
    </ResponsiveContainer>
  )
}
```

`<ResponsiveContainer>` makes the chart fill its parent width automatically — no fixed pixel widths needed. On mobile, enable horizontal scroll by wrapping the chart in an `overflow-x: auto` container so the 24-hour spread remains readable.

Set `interval={3}` on `<XAxis>` to show a tick every 3 hours instead of every hour, which prevents label overlap.

title: URL Shortener with Analytics
description: A URL shortening service with click tracking. The frontend developer builds the shortening UI, QR code generation, and an analytics dashboard. The backend developer builds the redirect API, slug generation, and click-tracking pipeline.

requirements.body: Shorten any valid URL to a 6–8 character slug
Support optional custom slugs with uniqueness validation
Redirect short URLs with HTTP 302 and record each click
Per-link analytics: total clicks, clicks over time, top referrers
Generate a downloadable QR code for each short URL
Redirect endpoint must respond in under 100ms (p99)
Rate-limit link creation to 10 per minute per IP
Slug lookup table must use a database index
API contract documented with a Postman collection or OpenAPI spec

items: Build the shortening form with URL validation and clipboard copy button
Render a QR code for each shortened URL using qrcode.react
Build the analytics dashboard: total clicks chart and referrer breakdown
Display a table of all user-created links with live click counts
Generate collision-free slugs with nanoid and store in PostgreSQL
Implement the redirect endpoint (GET /:slug) with 302 response
Record each click: timestamp, referrer header, user-agent
Expose analytics aggregation endpoints for the FE dashboard
Add a unique index on the slugs column and benchmark redirect latency
Define the API contract (slug format, error codes) before either side starts
Review and integrate both FE and BE implementations
Write end-to-end integration tests covering the full redirect + analytics flow
Set up a shared deployment pipeline

steps.title: Define the API contract before writing any code
steps.body:
Both developers agree on every endpoint before writing code. Write this document and sign off on it:

```http
POST /links
Body:     { url: string, customSlug?: string }
Response: 201 { id, slug, shortUrl }

GET /:slug
Response: 302 → original URL

GET /links
Response: [{ id, slug, shortUrl, originalUrl, totalClicks, createdAt }]

GET /links/:id/analytics
Response: { totalClicks, clicksPerDay: [{date, count}], topReferrers: [{domain, count}] }
```

Agree on error codes and slug format before either developer writes a line. Mismatched assumptions here cause the most wasted time on duo projects.

steps.title: Set up the database schema
steps.body:
Create two tables and add a unique index on the slug column.

```sql
CREATE TABLE links (
  id           UUID         PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  slug         VARCHAR(10)  UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  original_url TEXT         NOT NULL,
  created_by   INTEGER      REFERENCES users(id),
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE clicks (
  id         UUID        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  link_id    UUID        NOT NULL REFERENCES links(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  clicked_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
  referrer   TEXT,
  user_agent TEXT
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_links_slug ON links (slug);
```

The index on `slug` is what makes the redirect fast. Without it, every redirect does a full table scan.

steps.title: Build slug generation
Build the redirect endpoint
Build analytics aggregation
steps.body:
Write these as SQL aggregation queries — do not fetch all rows and aggregate in JavaScript.

```sql
-- Total clicks
SELECT COUNT(*)::int AS total_clicks
FROM clicks WHERE link_id = $1;

-- Clicks per day (last 30 days)
SELECT DATE(clicked_at) AS date, COUNT(*)::int AS count
FROM clicks
WHERE link_id = $1
  AND clicked_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY DATE(clicked_at)
ORDER BY date ASC;

-- Top referrers
SELECT COALESCE(referrer, 'Direct') AS domain,
       COUNT(*)::int AS count
FROM clicks WHERE link_id = $1
GROUP BY referrer
ORDER BY count DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

SQL aggregation is orders of magnitude faster than fetching all rows and computing in JavaScript. Expose these as `GET /links/:id/analytics` returning `{ totalClicks, clicksPerDay, topReferrers }`.

steps.title: Add validation and rate limiting
Build the shortening form
Generate and display the QR code
Build the analytics dashboard
steps.body:
Create an `AnalyticsPage` that fetches `GET /links/:id/analytics` and visualises the data with Recharts. ```jsx import { LineChart, Line, BarChart, Bar, XAxis, YAxis, Tooltip, ResponsiveContainer } from 'recharts' function AnalyticsPage({ linkId }) { // ... fetch data from GET /links/:id/analytics ... return (

{data.totalClicks} total clicks

) } ``` Show skeleton loaders while fetching and an empty state if `totalClicks === 0`.

steps.title: Build the links table
steps.body:
Fetch `GET /links` and render a table sorted by `created_at` descending.

Columns: Short URL (clickable), Original URL (truncated to 40 chars), Total Clicks, Created Date.

Each row needs:
- A copy button in the Short URL column (`navigator.clipboard.writeText`)
- A link to that link's analytics page

For truncation: `url.length > 40 ? url.slice(0, 40) + '…' : url`. Show the full URL in a tooltip on hover using the HTML `title` attribute.

Include:
- Authentication requirements

Commit this file to the repo. Your partner and future maintainers should be able to understand the entire API without reading the code.

title: Auth System from Scratch
description: Implement a production-grade authentication system: JWT access tokens stored only in memory, httpOnly refresh tokens with rotation, and role-based access control. One developer owns the backend; the other owns the React integration.

requirements.body: Register and login endpoints returning a short-lived JWT access token
Refresh token stored as bcrypt/SHA-256 hash in DB; rotated on every use
Refresh token delivered only via httpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie
Role-based access control: three roles; endpoints enforce required role
Logout invalidates the refresh token in the database
Silent refresh: React restores session on page reload without flashing login
Access tokens expire in 15 minutes; refresh tokens expire in 7 days
Login and register endpoints rate-limited to 5 req/min per IP
Timing-safe credential comparison (no username enumeration)
All security decisions documented in an ADR (Architecture Decision Record)

items: Implement AuthContext: access token lives only in module memory, never localStorage
Build the silent refresh interceptor in axios (deduplicate concurrent 401s)
Create a ProtectedRoute component that redirects unauthenticated users
Add role-based conditional rendering in the UI
Handle the session-expired UX: clear state and redirect to login gracefully
Implement JWT sign/verify with a per-environment secret (≥256 bits)
Build refresh token rotation: generate → hash → store → verify → rotate
Create an authenticate preHandler using request.jwtVerify()
Write a requireRole(roles[]) preHandler factory for RBAC enforcement
Add bcrypt-based password hashing with ≥12 rounds and constant-time comparison
Design the full token lifecycle and document the security model
Review implementation against the OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet
Coordinate the FE/BE token handoff: access token in response body, refresh in cookie
Write end-to-end tests: register → login → refresh → logout → verify cookie cleared
Produce a concise ADR covering every security trade-off made

resources.label: jwt.io — Introduction to JSON Web Tokens

steps.title: Read OWASP before touching code
steps.body:
Both developers read the OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet in full before writing a single line. This is not optional.

Every decision in this project — token expiry, cookie flags, hashing rounds, timing-safe comparison — has a documented security reason. You need to understand why, not just what.

Bookmark the cheat sheet; you will refer back to it during the security review in Step 14.

steps.title: Design the full token lifecycle on paper
steps.body:
Draw two flows before opening your editor.

**Flow 1 — Login:**
register → login → access token returned in body → React stores in module memory → refresh token set as httpOnly cookie

**Flow 2 — Silent refresh:**
API call returns 401 → React sends `POST /auth/refresh` with cookie → server rotates token → new access token returned → original request retried automatically

If you cannot draw both flows clearly, you are not ready to code. The interceptor in Step 10 implements Flow 2 exactly.

steps.title: Set up the database schema
steps.body:
Create the two tables. Never store the raw refresh token — only its SHA-256 hash.

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id            SERIAL       PRIMARY KEY,
  email         VARCHAR(255) UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  role          VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 'viewer',
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE refresh_tokens (
  id          UUID        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     INTEGER     NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  token_hash  CHAR(64)    NOT NULL,
  expires_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE INDEX idx_refresh_tokens_hash ON refresh_tokens (token_hash);
```

The index on `token_hash` is queried on every token refresh — without it each refresh call does a full table scan.

steps.title: Implement registration
Implement login and token issuance
Implement refresh token rotation
Implement logout and RBAC
Add rate limiting and timing safety
Build AuthContext with in-memory token storage
Build the silent refresh axios interceptor
Build ProtectedRoute and role-based rendering
Write end-to-end tests for the full auth lifecycle
steps.body:
Write one test suite covering the complete lifecycle in order.

```
1. Register a new user              → expect 201
2. Login                            → expect access token in body, cookie set
3. Call a protected endpoint        → expect 200
4. POST /auth/refresh               → expect new access token + new cookie value
5. Retry with the old cookie value  → expect 401 (token was rotated)
6. Logout                           → expect cookie is cleared
7. Call protected endpoint with old token → expect 401
```

All 7 assertions must pass. These are your regression tests — if any breaks during refactoring, the auth system has regressed.

steps.title: Write the ADR
steps.body:
Create `docs/auth-adr.md`. Document every security decision with its rationale:

- Why httpOnly cookie for the refresh token (not localStorage)
- Why 15-minute access token expiry
- Why SHA-256 for the stored token hash (not bcrypt)
- Why SameSite=Strict on the cookie
- Why token rotation on every refresh
- Why constant-time comparison for credentials

An ADR is not a tutorial — it records decisions and their trade-offs so future developers do not undo them unknowingly.

steps.title: Security review against OWASP
steps.body:
Go through the OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet line by line. For each item, mark it as: implemented, not applicable, or a known gap. Fix all gaps.

Common misses at this stage:
- Password complexity not enforced
- Refresh token not invalidated on password change
- JWT algorithm not explicitly set to `HS256` (leaving it open to the `none` algorithm attack)
- Session not fully invalidated on logout (all refresh tokens for the user should be cleared)

Do not ship without a completed review.

title: Real-time Collaboration Tool
description: A shared document editor with real-time cursor presence, conflict-free merging (CRDT via Yjs), and offline buffering. Three roles collaborate: frontend owns the editor integration, backend owns the WebSocket server, fullstack designs the protocol and writes the integration tests.

requirements.body: Multiple users can edit the same document simultaneously in real time

Implement WebSocket client lifecycle: connect, reconnect, backoff strategy

Lead the end-to-end system review and sign off on the security model

steps.title: Read Yjs and understand CRDTs before any code
steps.body:
All three team members read docs.yjs.dev in full before writing any code.

Understand these core concepts before you start:
- `Y.Doc` — the shared data structure. Every collaborator holds a copy.
- `Y.Text` — the collaborative text type. Changes are operations, not replacements.
- `Y.Awareness` — for presence data: cursors, names, online status.
- Updates are binary-encoded and can be applied in any order — this is what makes conflict resolution automatic.

If you do not understand why order does not matter, read crdt.tech first. If you skip this step, you will spend days debugging merge bugs that the library already solves.

steps.title: Design and sign off on the WebSocket message protocol
Set up the database schema
steps.body:
Create three tables. The `yjs_state` columns store binary-encoded Yjs document state.

```sql
CREATE TABLE documents (
  id         UUID        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  title      TEXT        NOT NULL,
  yjs_state  BYTEA,
  updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE snapshots (
  id          UUID        PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  document_id UUID        NOT NULL REFERENCES documents(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  yjs_state   BYTEA       NOT NULL,
  label       TEXT,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()
);

CREATE TABLE document_members (
  document_id UUID    NOT NULL REFERENCES documents(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  user_id     INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  joined_at   TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW(),
  PRIMARY KEY (document_id, user_id)
);
```

The `BYTEA` columns hold `Y.encodeStateAsUpdate(doc)` output — a compact binary diff that reconstructs the full document state when applied to any empty `Y.Doc`.

steps.title: Build the authenticated WebSocket upgrade
Implement room-based broadcasting
Integrate Yjs server-side and handle sync

Set up CodeMirror 6 with the Yjs binding
steps.body:
Install the packages and create the editor with the Yjs collaborative binding.

```bash
npm install yjs y-codemirror.next codemirror @codemirror/lang-javascript
```

```js
import * as Y from 'yjs'
import { yCollab } from 'y-codemirror.next'
import { EditorView, basicSetup } from 'codemirror'
import { javascript } from '@codemirror/lang-javascript'

const ydoc      = new Y.Doc()
const ytext     = ydoc.getText('codemirror')
const awareness = new Y.Awareness(ydoc)

const view = new EditorView({
  extensions: [
    basicSetup,
    javascript(),
    yCollab(ytext, awareness)
  ],
  parent: document.getElementById('editor')
})
```

Before wiring up the WebSocket, open two browser tabs on the same page and verify that typing in one updates the other — they share the same `ydoc` in memory. Understanding local sync first prevents confusing local bugs with network bugs.

steps.title: Connect to the server with y-websocket
Build the presence overlay
Test offline buffering
steps.body:
y-websocket buffers local Yjs updates while disconnected and flushes them on reconnect. Verify this manually before writing tests:

1. Open the app in two browser tabs
2. In Chrome DevTools, take one tab offline: Network → No throttling → Offline
3. Make edits in both tabs
4. Bring the offline tab back online
5. Both tabs should converge to the same document state within a few seconds

If they do not converge, you have a server-side merge bug — check that `Y.applyUpdate` is being called on the server doc in the `update` message handler.

steps.title: Build version history
Write multi-client integration tests
steps.body:
Simulate two WebSocket clients connecting to the same document in a test environment.

Test scenarios to cover:
1. Client A types 'hello', Client B types 'world' simultaneously → both see the merged result
2. Client B disconnects, Client A makes 5 edits, Client B reconnects → B receives all 5 edits
3. Network split: both clients make concurrent edits offline → on reconnect, neither loses changes

Assert that both clients end up with identical document text after every scenario. Identical text from two CRDTs is the proof of correctness — if they diverge, `Y.applyUpdate` is being called incorrectly on the server.

steps.title: Load test and hit the 50ms latency target
steps.body:
Use autocannon or k6 to open 100 concurrent WebSocket connections to one document. Have each connection send an update every second. Measure time from send to receive on the other connections (add a timestamp to each update payload).

Target: p99 latency under 50ms.

Common bottlenecks:
- Synchronous JSON serialisation in the broadcast loop — use binary Yjs updates directly
- Unindexed database queries on the hot path
- Redis round-trips on every single message — batch or pipeline them

Profile before optimising — do not guess where the bottleneck is.

steps.title: Security review
steps.body:
Check four things before shipping:

1. **JWT validated on every upgrade** — try connecting with an expired token and assert the connection is rejected with close code 4001
2. **User cannot set another user's awareness state** — the server should overwrite the `user` field in awareness payloads with the server-verified identity, not trust what the client sends
3. **Snapshot restore requires membership** — test restoring a document with a different user's token, assert 403
4. **Redis channel names are not guessable** — channels are `doc:<uuid>`, not `doc:<sequential-id>`. UUIDs are not enumerable; sequential IDs are.
